title: A task-family model of within-person fMRI connectivity differences from 30 OpenNeuro studies transfers weakly to held-out studies
abstract: When one person does two kinds of fMRI task, the correlation pattern between brain regions differs between the runs, and the direction of this difference for a pair of task families is partly the same in independent studies. This matters because it shows a shared, family-specific part of task connectivity across scanners, labs and task versions, and it shows which nominal task categories behave as one family. We used ReadyNeuro, minimally preprocessed OpenNeuro fMRI. For each run we computed functional connectivity (FC), the correlation between the signals of 100 cortical regions (4,950 region pairs), and we coded each task label into a family (for example working memory, cognitive control, reward, emotion, language). Inside each person we compared runs of different families, so that person, scanner and acquisition cancel. A model of family effects fitted on 30 discovery studies (62 people) predicted the within-person FC differences in 30 held-out studies (76 people, 23 study groups). In the pre-registered primary test (pairs of two trial-based families), the correlation between the observed and the predicted differences was +0.030 (95% CI +0.011 to +0.049; Cohen d 0.69; positive in 16 of 23 groups; p = 0.0016). Rest versus task (+0.116), FC after global-signal regression (+0.042) and 21 network-level FC values (+0.137) also transferred. After regression of a canonical model of each run's event design the transfer stayed the same (+0.032, 15 groups, p = 0.04); covariates for head motion and run length did not change it. The effect was weaker in the randomly assigned confirmation studies (+0.021, p = 0.09) and in the reverse direction (+0.017, p = 0.14). In exploratory analyses that held out studies with shared localizer protocols together, emotion, working-memory, control and language tasks matched their own family in new studies, but reward and episodic-memory tasks were not detected as coherent families, and the part of the within-study reproducible difference that was shared across protocols was small (about 20%, 95% CI -7% to 50%). Limitations: task labels only, so evoked activity can remain in the connectivity; 1-5 people per study; small absolute effects; one coder for the task families.

citations.reason: Campaign branch A4 (patterns along the condition); this work is on leaf task-space.

Same leaf. It reported that trial tasks of different cognitive families did not separate on a task-minus-rest map with 1-3 people per study. Our within-person task-versus-task test qualifies this: in connectivity they separate weakly in held-out studies.
We used its list of accession pairs with copied runs to check that no such pair crosses our discovery/confirmation halves.
